title: The Lord's dog
hookLine: Kabir calls himself the Lord's dog, with a chain round his neck, going where He leads (Kabir salok, ang 1368)

lines: IT KNOWS WHOSE HAND IT IS.
cards: Early morning, any street. A dog trots ahead of its person, nose down, tail up, stopping at every post. Then a gentle tug on the leash, and the dog turns, without fuss, and goes the other way.
It doesn't sulk. It doesn't argue. It knows whose hand is on the other end.
Kabir saw that too, and put himself in the picture. In one of his saloks he doesn't call himself a saint, or a seeker, or even a weaver. He gives himself a name, and a collar.

teach.h: MOTI: A PEARL, A PET'S NAME.
teach.b: Kabir, I am the Lord's dog, and Moti is my name.

teach.h: WHEREVER HE PULLS ME, I GO.
teach.b: There's a cord around my neck; wherever He pulls me, I go. Moti means pearl. It's a pet's name, the kind you'd call across a yard.
So Kabir isn't only lowering himself here. He's also saying he's loved: a dog with a name belongs to someone.
Calling yourself a dog was no flattering thing, and Kabir chose it anyway, with a little warmth and maybe a little humor. Yesterday he said, I am the worst of all.
Today the feeling has shifted, less about faults and more about trust. A dog on a leash isn't ashamed. It's attached.
The chain could sound like a prison. But listen to who's holding it, and how Kabir answers: wherever He pulls me, I go. No complaint in it.
The chain is what keeps him near.
Sikh teachers connect this with hukam, the Divine will, and the Gurus' call to walk in it. Not dragged, but led.
There's even relief in it. A dog doesn't have to plan the whole walk; it only has to feel the next tug and follow. Kabir doesn't pretend the leash isn't there.
He just knows whose hand it's in.

how: Sikhs read Kabir's saloks near the end of the Guru Granth Sahib, and teachers use this one to speak of hukam, walking in the Divine will with trust rather than resistance.

o: pearl, the pet's name Kabir gives himself
a stray dog with no owner to follow
a chain or cord around a dog's neck

games.q: the Lord's dog — tap the pairs.

s: in the salok, the dog has no name
Kabir names himself Moti, pearl, a pet's name.
the salok complains about the chain
there's no complaint: wherever He pulls me, I go.
Sikh teachers connect this salok with hukam, the Divine will

games.q: you're Kabir, looking for a picture of how you walk with the Lord. what do you call yourself?
o: the Lord's dog, with a cord on my neck.
a lone traveler with a map.
games.why: the Lord's dog, named Moti: wherever He pulls me, I go. lowly, and loved.

practice: Think of a small good nudge you've been feeling and ignoring: call your grandmother, drink some water, apologize, go to bed earlier.
Don't plan the whole walk; just feel the next small step and agree to it, breathing easy, like a dog trotting beside someone it trusts. If you pray, you can say Waheguru, and let it be your yes.

wordCard.voice: Moti. The pet's name Kabir gives himself in his salok: a pearl, with a cord around his neck, going wherever the Lord pulls.

orig.note: Punjabi, in Gurmukhi, as Kabir's salok writes it: a dog.

carryVoice: Your line: led by the chain. Close enough to feel the next tug. Day seven hundred fifty-five.

sources.ref: Guru Granth Sahib, Salok Kabir, Ang 1368 ('I am the Lord's dog; Moti is my name; a cord around my neck; wherever He pulls me, I go')
